title: What Data Is and How Programs Represent It
learningObjectives: Explain what data represents in a program and why it is needed.
Distinguish raw data from meaningful information produced by processing.
Describe how programs store and represent different kinds of values.
Identify how the same real-world fact may have different representations.
Explain why representation choices affect interpretation, storage, operations, and correctness.

understand.concept: Data is a representation of facts, measurements, observations, choices, or instructions that a program can work with. A program does not directly understand a real-world object or idea; it operates on representations such as numbers, text, true/false values, identifiers, and structured records. The same fact can be represented in different ways, and the representation determines what operations are meaningful.
understand.whyItMatters: Every program receives, stores, transforms, and produces data. Understanding representation helps prevent errors such as treating a postal code as a number to calculate with, confusing a text digit with a numeric value, or losing meaning during conversion.
understand.analogy: A library catalog card represents a book—it is not the book itself. A program uses representations in a similar way: a value stands for something the program needs to reason about.
understand.analogyLimit: Representations can be incomplete, rounded, encoded, or constrained. They may not preserve every detail of the real-world thing they describe.

explain.narrative: Begin by asking what a value stands for, not only what characters appear on screen. The text '42' could be a quantity, a code, a label, or a number of years. A numeric value can be used in arithmetic, while an identifier may need to preserve formatting such as leading zeros. Data representation is a model of the information a task needs; choosing a model deliberately makes operations and validation easier.

examples.title: A numeric quantity
examples.explanation: Value represents countable units; arithmetic such as stock - 1 may be meaningful.

examples.title: Text that looks numeric
examples.explanation: As text, leading zeros are preserved and the value is not treated as a quantity.

examples.title: A Boolean status
examples.explanation: A true/false representation captures a yes/no state; it is not the same as the words 'false' stored as text.

examples.title: Date represented as components
examples.explanation: Separate components make each part explicit, but require rules for valid combinations and ordering.

examples.title: Transform raw data into information
examples.code: let prices = [10, 15, 20]; let total = prices.reduce((a,b) => a+b, 0);
examples.explanation: The individual values are data; their calculated sum answers a question about the data.

commonMistakes: Assuming every digit-only value should be numeric.
Confusing a value's display form with its internal representation.
Using a representation that cannot preserve required precision or formatting.
Ignoring the meaning and constraints of the real-world value.
Assuming a stored value is automatically accurate or trustworthy.

guidedTask.title: Guided: Choose and explain a representation
guidedTask.instructions: Use the lesson ideas to analyze the task "What Data Is and How Programs Represent It". For each case, identify the value(s), what they represent, and the operation or type behavior that matters.
steps: State what each data item represents in the real-world task.
Choose a representation and justify why it preserves the needed information.
Identify a valid operation and one operation that should be avoided or checked.
Describe one edge case or conversion risk.
Summarize what a learner should verify in the language they are using.
guidedTask.starterCode: // Write notes or a small example that demonstrates the lesson concept

independentTask.title: Independent: Data and type decision notes
independentTask.instructions: Create three examples from a simple application and explain the data representation choices.
requirements: Include one simple value and one composite value.
Explain the purpose of each representation.
Show one assignment or operation and predict its behavior.
Identify one likely mistake or boundary case.
Explain any language-specific rule you would verify rather than assume.

hints: Begin with the meaning of the value, not its appearance.
Ask whether arithmetic, ordering, formatting, or grouping is required.
Keep identifiers and quantities conceptually distinct.
Composite data groups related values; references may allow sharing.
Check the target language's actual assignment, conversion, and type-checking rules.
